Write a GLSL ES 3.00 fragment shader for my tabletop RPG VTT, Gravewright.

It is drawn into its own rectangular frame, placed above the map and below the darkness layer, and it is a generative shader: it paints the effect itself and the map shows through its alpha, so always write to finalColor with the colour already multiplied by alpha, as vec4(colour * a, a). Do not try to read the scene image, because it never reaches you: uTexture is the frame's own texture. You also need not clip the effect: the frame is already the size of the range and is clipped by the visibility polygon traced from the origin, so walls and closed doors stop the effect before your code is involved. Paint freely to the edges.

What matters for the drawing to land correctly is the space you work in. Do not build the pattern on raw vTextureCoord, because that pins the drawing to the screen and makes the map slide under it whenever someone zooms or pans. Use gwPattern(vTextureCoord), which returns that pixel's world position already rotated by the rotation slider and correctly scaled: it ties the drawing size to the range, so a small circle shows as much pattern as a large one instead of one flat patch. If you need the raw point, gwWorld and gwRotated are still there, and gwFeature() returns the characteristic size in world units. A grid cell is about 70 world units. If you want the effect to answer the lighting, call gwLight(vTextureCoord): it returns the light reaching that pixel, with the accumulated colour of the sources in rgb and the intensity in alpha, already clipped by walls: near a torch the effect should warm up and brighten, and in the dark it should nearly vanish.

You need not declare any of the following, because the preamble already provides it:
  in vec2 vTextureCoord;
  out vec4 finalColor;
  uniform sampler2D uTexture;      // the frame's OWN texture, not the scene
  uniform sampler2D uLightBuffer;  // scene light, already clipped by walls
  uniform float uTime;             // seconds
  uniform float uIntensity;
  uniform float uScale;
  uniform float uSpeed;
  uniform vec3 uColor;
  uniform vec2 uResolution;        // frame size, in pixels
  uniform float uAspect;
  uniform vec2 uOrigin;            // effect origin, in WORLD coordinates
  uniform float uRadius;           // range in world units (0 = whole scene)
  uniform float uRotation;         // radians
  uniform vec3 uCamera;            // (offset x, offset y, zoom)
  uniform vec2 uScreen;            // screen size, in pixels
  vec2 gwScreen(vec2 uv);          // this pixel's screen position, in pixels
  float gwFeature();               // pattern size in world units, already tied to the range
  vec2 gwPattern(vec2 uv);         // world point, rotated and correctly scaled: build on this one
  vec2 gwWorld(vec2 uv);           // this pixel's world position
  vec2 gwRotated(vec2 uv);         // the same point, rotated around uOrigin
  vec2 gwScreenUV(vec2 uv);        // screen position, 0..1
  vec4 gwLight(vec2 uv);           // light reaching here: rgb = colour, a = intensity

RANGES THE ENGINE ACCEPTS (respect them: out-of-range values are clamped, and the effect comes out different from what you pictured)
  uIntensity  0.0 to 1.0       (step 0.05)
  uScale      0.1 to 20.0      (step 0.1)
  uSpeed      0.0 to 8.0       (step 0.1): 0 freezes the effect
  uRotation   0 to 359 degrees, delivered in radians
  uColor      0.0 to 1.0 per channel
  range       0 to 120 cells   (0 = whole scene, with no wall occlusion)
